task.description: WF-03 Step 0.5 (registry lookup) and Step 1 (diagnose) for ISS-0446, per docs/agents/workflows/WF-03_issue_resolving.md. Verify the issue's root-cause reading against real ExUnit source (not memory), evaluate all four candidate remedies including ORCH's added fourth (start_supervised/start_supervised!), make a sizing call, and respect the evidence caveat that a green local run is not evidence given this is a timing-dependent race.

result.summary:
STEP 0.5 REGISTRY LOOKUP: grepped docs/issues/*.yaml for on_exit/Supervisor.stop/check-then-act/teardown-race entries. No resolved entry matches this symptom (checked ISS-0048, 0064, 0109, 0112, 0116, 0217, 0260, 0409, 0410, 0414, 0418, plus every resolved hit for 'teardown' generally) -- all are unrelated (schema/tenant/other teardown classes). This is a first occurrence, not a recurrence; severity stays as filed (MINOR).

STEP 1 DIAGNOSIS.

(1) THE ISSUE'S ROOT-CAUSE READING IS CONFIRMED, mechanism verified against real ExUnit 1.20.3 source read from /c/Program Files/Elixir/lib/ex_unit (not memory) and empirically reproduced. Exact call chain, cited by line:
  - ex_unit/lib/ex_unit/runner.ex:441-469 spawn_test_monitor/4: the TEST PROCESS is a freshly spawned process (test_pid) that registers itself with ExUnit.OnExitHandler.register(self()) (line 449), runs setup+body, then at line 466-467 sends {self(), :test_finished, test} to parent_pid (the ExUnit RUNNER process, a DIFFERENT process) and immediately calls exit(:shutdown) -- terminating itself right there.
  - runner.ex:496-523 receive_test_reply/4 (running in the RUNNER process, not the test process) blocks on that :test_finished message, then runner.ex:433-438 spawn_test/3 calls exec_on_exit(test, test_pid, timeout) -> runner.ex:540 exec_on_exit/3 calls ExUnit.OnExitHandler.run(pid, timeout) with pid = test_pid.
  - on_exit_handler.ex:52-57 run/2 takes the registered on_exit callbacks and calls exec_on_exit_callbacks -> exec_on_exit_callback (line 87) -> ensure_alive_callback_runner (line 131-133) which does spawn_monitor(__MODULE__, :on_exit_runner_loop, []) -- THE ON_EXIT CALLBACK BODY RUNS IN YET A THIRD, FRESHLY SPAWNED PROCESS, never in the test process itself.
  So by the time the on_exit callback executes: the test process (which owned the link to sup_pid, since Supervisor.start_link/2 was called from inside the test body) has already sent its finished-message and is calling/has called exit(:shutdown); the callback itself runs in an unrelated process with no link relationship to sup_pid at all. The supervisor's actual death is driven purely by the link-exit signal propagating asynchronously from the now-exiting test process -- there is no synchronization at all between 'test process's exit signal reaches sup_pid' and 'on_exit callback's Process.alive?(sup_pid) check', which is exactly the unordered race the issue describes. Supervisor.stop/3 is confirmed at elixir/lib/supervisor.ex:1197 to be literally `GenServer.stop(supervisor, reason, timeout)`, matching the CI stacktrace's GenServer.stop/3 -> :sys.terminate -> EXIT shutdown exactly.
  EMPIRICAL REPRODUCTION (throwaway scripts in scratch/, deleted after use, git status clean): a minimal repro with an instantly-terminating supervisor showed Process.alive?(sup_pid) = false 10/10 runs (stop/1 never reached with a live pid -> :noproc, not the CI's :shutdown -- this narrower shape does NOT match CI). Widening the window with a child GenServer whose terminate/2 does real work (Process.sleep(5)) reproduced the CI failure's EXACT shape 5/5 runs: Process.alive?(sup_pid) = true, then Supervisor.stop(sup_pid) raised exactly `{:shutdown, {:sys, :terminate, [...]}}` matching the observed CI exit reason and stacktrace. This confirms the race requires the supervisor/its children to take measurable time to actually terminate after the link signal -- which loaded, contended CI hardware makes far more likely than a quiet local run, matching the issue's own observation that this reproduces on CI but not locally.
  CAVEAT ON THE ISSUE'S WORDING: the issue says 'the supervisor is already terminating when on_exit runs' as if on_exit always runs after test-process exit has started. More precisely: on_exit's callback runs in a separate process with NO ordering guarantee relative to the link-exit signal's delivery to sup_pid at all -- it can run before, during, or after. The three-probe reproduction above demonstrates the 'during' case reproduces the exact CI symptom; the issue's overall claim (this is an unsynchronized check-then-act race across a process boundary, inherent to guarding a linked process this way) is CONFIRMED, not refuted, but the finer claim of a fixed before/after ordering is not quite right -- there is no ordering guarantee in either direction, which if anything makes the race MORE certain to eventually manifest, not less.

(2) ALL FOUR OPTIONS EVALUATED.
  (a) DROP THE on_exit ENTIRELY -- VERIFIED, not assumed, per the issue's own instruction to verify before relying on it. Empirical test (ExUnit.run() driven synchronously in a throwaway script, ETS-backed watcher process independent of the test process): with NO on_exit callback at all, a named supervisor + named child both received {:DOWN, ..., :shutdown} from pure link-propagated teardown once the test process called exit(:shutdown) -- 100% clean, no leaked process. A second empirical test ran two sequential (async: false) tests that both register the SAME name (__MODULE__.Sup): test B's Supervisor.start_link with that name succeeded cleanly 3/3 runs with no {:already_started, pid} collision, confirming the ExUnit runner's own serialization (receive_test_reply blocks on :test_finished, which the test process sends only after its exit(:shutdown) call is imminent, and the runner does not dispatch the next test until exec_on_exit/the current test's full lifecycle completes) means the linked supervisor and its registered name are always fully torn down before the next test in sequence starts. CONCLUSION: the on_exit callback is REDUNDANT for this test as currently written (Supervisor.start_link/2 with no name isolation trick, no explicit ownership transfer) -- Process.alive?(pid) inside the test body still works because the check happens before the test process itself exits. Dropping the on_exit removes the race with no loss of cleanup guarantee AND leaves the registered name (__MODULE__.ThrowawaySupervisor) fully released before the next test file/case runs, addressing the leak concern the task explicitly asked about.
  (b) RACE-TOLERANT EXPLICIT STOP -- viable as a fallback but weaker than (a). Wrapping Supervisor.stop/1 in try/catch :exit and treating :noproc/:shutdown as success would eliminate the crash, but it keeps an on_exit callback that does no useful additional cleanup beyond what link-teardown already guarantees (per (a)'s finding) -- it would be added ceremony that tolerates a race rather than removing it, and per the sizing question below, this is the '2>&1 masking a gate' smell in miniature: catching a symptom rather than removing its cause. Also: no in-suite precedent exists for this shape (confirmed by ORCH's Step 00 grep -- Supervisor.stop/1 is not called anywhere else in test/), so choosing (b) would newly establish a pattern rather than follow one.
  (c) UNLINKED / TEST-OWNED SUPERVISOR (start_link then Process.unlink, or a supervised start under a test-owned supervisor) -- viable, removes the race by removing the link (an unlinked sup_pid does not die from the test process's exit at all, so an explicit stop is then unambiguously required, since nothing else will clean it up), but this is MORE code than (a), introduces a new manual-unlink idiom with no in-suite precedent, and re-introduces the need for exactly the explicit-stop step whose failure mode is what caused this issue -- unless that stop is ALSO written race-tolerant, which folds this into (b)'s ceremony anyway.
  (d) start_supervised/start_supervised! (ORCH's added fourth option, WF-03's in-suite-precedent instinct) -- ALSO VERIFIED against real source, not assumed. ex_unit/lib/ex_unit/callbacks.ex:568-580 start_supervised/2 fetches ExUnit.fetch_test_supervisor() and calls Supervisor.start_child on THAT framework-owned supervisor -- the child is never given its own ad-hoc Supervisor.start_link/2 call at all, so there is no user-managed sup_pid and no user-written on_exit in the first place. Teardown of ExUnit's OWN test supervisor happens via on_exit_handler.ex:59-70 terminate_supervisor/2, which uses Process.monitor(sup) + receive {:DOWN, ...} -- an atomic monitor-wait, structurally immune to the check-then-act race by construction, because there is no Process.alive? check at all, only a blocking wait for the actual death signal. This is the strongest structural fix and matches the established in-suite precedent at test/letflow/admission_test.exs:19 and test/letflow/scheduler/poller_test.exs:148,400. HOWEVER: it does not literally fit this test's own shape without a design decision -- the test starts the CHILD SPEC UNDER A SUPERVISOR IT CONTROLS specifically to exercise Supervisor.which_children/1 against that supervisor's own child list (asserting the exact {module, pid, :worker, modules} tuple), which start_supervised!/2 does not give you access to (it returns only the child pid, not a supervisor whose children you enumerate) -- so adopting (d) verbatim would require either dropping the which_children/1 assertion (weakening what this specific test proves, since that assertion is what makes it 'independently startable under a throwaway supervisor' rather than just 'startable') or a different structural approach (e.g. still using an explicit Supervisor.start_link/2 for the which_children/1 assertion, but relying on (a)'s finding that no on_exit is needed for it). This is a real design tradeoff, not a wash -- CODE-DESIGNER should decide whether (d)'s teardown-safety is worth restructuring the assertion, or whether (a) (same supervisor shape, on_exit simply removed) achieves the same safety with a strictly smaller diff and no loss of test coverage.

(3) SIZING CALL. This does NOT reduce to a one-line mechanical substitution that ORCH should apply directly, despite (a)'s finding sounding simple ('just delete three lines'). Two things keep it out of ORCH's direct-fix lane and in the full WF-03 chain, consistent with Step 00's own sizing verdict (which already routed this through the full chain and remains correct): first, ORCHESTRATOR.md section 10 check 6 (does the change alter asserted test behaviour) is not resolved by this diagnosis alone -- (a) requires deleting an on_exit block from a shipped test, and even though this diagnosis's own empirical probes show no coverage loss for THIS test's current assertions, confirming that for the ACTUAL test module (not a throwaway analog) and confirming no other test in the file/suite depends on ordering relative to this teardown is exactly the kind of check CODE-DESIGNER/TEST-DESIGNER should make explicit in a design and TEST-DESIGN-VALIDATOR should independently re-derive, per core-directives.md's validator principle -- an ISSUE-FIXER-authored probe against a throwaway analog script is not the same evidentiary weight as a design-gated change to the real shipped file. Second, there is a genuine, non-mechanical design decision open between (a) and (d) identified in (2) above (whether to restructure the which_children/1 assertion to gain (d)'s structural immunity, or keep the current shape and rely on (a)'s no-op-on_exit finding) -- 'genuinely equivalent options requiring a decision no agent can infer' is precisely the shape core-directives.md's Zero Manual Work section reserves for a design step, not silent ORCH judgement. RECOMMENDATION TO CODE-DESIGNER: option (a) (drop the on_exit) is the strongest default given the empirical evidence above -- it removes the race entirely (no check-then-act left to race), matches this test's own existing supervisor-ownership shape with the smallest diff, and requires no restructuring of the which_children/1 assertion. Do not adopt (b) or (c) without first re-examining why (a) does not suffice, since neither adds safety (a) doesn't already have and both add un-precedented ceremony. (d) is worth a brief comparative note in the design artefact but should not be force-fit if it requires weakening the which_children/1 assertion -- flag that tradeoff explicitly rather than silently picking a side.

(4) EVIDENCE CAVEAT RESPECTED. This diagnosis's confidence rests on: (i) real ExUnit/Supervisor source cited by exact file and line, not memory; (ii) a structural reproduction of the CI failure's exact exit shape (5/5) using an artificial widened-timing analog, which is legitimate as MECHANISM evidence (it shows the race class is real and reproducible under the right timing, which is what CI's loaded hardware supplies) but is NOT a claim that the actual shipped test file was run and failed/passed in this session -- it was not, deliberately, since (per the task's own instruction) a green run of the real timing-dependent race proves nothing. I did NOT run test/letflow/engine/service_task_dispatcher_test.exs itself in this diagnosis step (no fix exists yet to test, and a pre-fix green run would be exactly the false-confidence signal the task warned against) and I am not claiming any run result for it. The regression-proof obligation (fail pre-fix / pass post-fix, and per WF-03's own non-existence caveat this is NOT a non-existence case, so ordinary fail-then-pass applies) belongs to TEST-DESIGNER at Step 4, and given this is a genuinely intermittent race, TEST-DESIGNER will need a widened-timing analog similar to the one used here (a slow-terminating child under the throwaway supervisor) to make the pre-fix failure reliably reproducible rather than praying for CI-level contention locally -- recommend passing this diagnosis's probe technique (scratch script pattern: Supervisor.start_link with a child whose terminate/2 sleeps briefly) forward as a concrete suggestion for how to construct that fail-first proof deterministically.
